title: Why do taxi wars keep erupting and shutting down our roads?

scenes.label: killed in 3 weeks
lines: At least a dozen people have been killed in Cape Town in about three weeks.
They were shot at taxi ranks and on streets in places like Delft, Gugulethu and Khayelitsha.
Today, thousands of commuters were stranded, and even the airport was short of staff and slow.
Matric learners were sent to other exam centres.
So why do taxi wars keep coming back? Let's open the case.

scenes.headline: The Taxi Wars
lines: Case file: the taxi wars.

scenes.name: Thandiwe

bubbles.text: Thandiwe is an example, not a real person.
Will a taxi even come today?
If I'm late, I lose pay. If I walk, is it safe?

lines: Let's meet Thandiwe. She is an example, but her story is real for thousands of people.
She cleans offices in town, and leaves home at five every morning.
Today the taxis are slow, and she stands at the rank, not knowing if one will come.
If she is late, she may lose her pay. If she walks, it may not be safe.
To understand this, we go back to apartheid.
Before 1987, taxis were tightly controlled, and Black people were refused permits.
With no clear rules, competition grew for passengers and good routes, so operators joined together in groups called associations.
Two of them, CATA and CODETA, signed a peace agreement in 1996.
Peace is possible. From February 2010 to June 2012, not one taxi murder was reported in the Western Cape.
But in July 2021, the Mobility MEC at the time said twenty two people were murdered in sixteen days.
And now, in 2026, at least a dozen people have died in about three weeks.
Here is what the last few weeks look like.
EWN reports at least a dozen people killed in about three weeks, in places like Delft, Gugulethu, Khayelitsha and Bonteheuwel.
Other outlets give slightly different counts, so police still need to confirm the exact number.
Between Tuesday and Wednesday, nine people were shot in just twenty four hours, and three of them died.
Today the airport was short of staff, and travellers were told to arrive four hours early for international flights.

scenes.headline: What people are saying

items.text: This thing is out of our hands.
I call on taxi industry leaders to stop this
We need to protect the lives of our commuters
items.who: Isaac Sileku, WC Mobility MEC (Cape Times)

items.text: Why can't government just stop them?

lines: Everyone is asking the same thing: why can't this be stopped?
The taxi council itself says it is struggling.
The mayor is calling on taxi leaders to rise above the violence.
The province's Mobility MEC says he must protect commuters.
And many ordinary people just want a simple answer.

scenes.headline: Why it keeps happening

cards.title: Routes
cards.sub: Routes mean money, so groups fight

lines: So why does it keep happening? There are three main suspects.
Fights over routes and the money in them. Broken permits. And no consequences for the people behind it.

scenes.name: Sipho

bubbles.text: Sipho is an example, not a real person.
Those are my passengers. This is my route.
A route invasion: one group moves onto another's route.

lines: Meet Sipho, an example of a taxi driver.
For years his group has worked one route, and its passengers pay his wages.
Then taxis from another group start loading passengers at his rank.
That is called a route invasion, and it feels like someone taking food off his table.
This is how a fight over passengers can grow into a war between whole groups.
Suspect number one: routes, and the money in them.
The province has eight taxi regions.
Yet the Mobility MEC says that when there is a deadlock, it is always CATA and CODETA.
Taxis matter. An older figure says they carry about twenty nine percent of public transport users in the Western Cape.
The City says years of talks, and even the High Court, have not ended the route disputes in Delft, Khayelitsha and Somerset West.
The province names overtrading as a root cause. That means too many taxis chasing too few passengers.
Routes are lucrative, meaning they pay well. Control the route, the rank and the membership fees, and you control the money.
Suspect number two: permits.
An operating licence is the paper that lets a taxi work a route. Without it, a taxi has no legal right to be there.
In 2021, one operator told the Mail and Guardian he had six licences but thirty seven taxis on one route.
He said he could not get the support letter needed to apply for more. That is his own claim.
The MEC at the time said taxis were running illegally, allegedly with the blessing of leaders in some associations.
In Gauteng, a 2021 commission found weak licensing let people make fraudulent changes with help from officials.
Whether that happens in Cape Town is a question the province must answer.
A national system is meant to link licences to the vehicle database, so one licence cannot cover many taxis, but we could not confirm it is working here yet.

scenes.headline: Peace deals, then violence again
scenes.quote: In the past we have rewarded perpetrators of violence by issuing them with operating licence.
lines: Suspect number three: no consequences.
The province itself says the violence continues despite previous peace agreements.
In August 2025, at least six people died in four days. Now it is 2026.
The 2005 Ntsebeza inquiry found a culture of lawlessness, fear and silence, weak policing and hit squads.
It said the most damning failure was that those who plan and gain from the violence are not brought to justice.
In 2018, the FW de Klerk Foundation wrote that there was no evidence its advice was followed. We found no recent official check.
And the Mobility Department admits a past failing, in its own words.
So who is actually in charge? The honest answer is: many hands.
The province issues licences, and under a law called Section 91 it can close routes and ranks when lives are at risk.
The City of Cape Town runs the ranks, plus law enforcement and cameras.
The police investigate, through a Provincial Taxi Violence Unit.
SANTACO, the national taxi council, admits it cannot guarantee commuter safety.
A 2021 analysis spoke of regulatory failings and blame-shifting between these bodies.
Now, why do whole roads shut down, not just one rank?
First, the fighting itself. On Thursday the R300 was closed after a shooting believed to be taxi-related.
Today an unofficial go-slow left thousands of commuters stranded.
Second, the government's own tool. In September 2025 the province closed routes for thirty days, because lives were at risk.
It worked for a while. No new violent incidents were reported in the first ten days.
But thousands lost their daily commute, and COSATU said it was done without enough consultation or a clear plan for workers.
A year later, the violence is back, so closing routes did not settle the dispute.

scenes.headline: Where did the taxi money go?
lines: Many people ask: how much is spent on stopping this, and is it working?
We found no budget line for taxi violence policing or mediation, so we followed the biggest national taxi spend instead.
It is the taxi recapitalisation programme, which pays owners to scrap old taxis.
Cabinet approved seven point seven billion rand over seven years to scrap one hundred thousand taxis. That is about seventy seven thousand rand for each taxi.
The Transport Minister told Parliament in September 2025 that eighty five thousand nine hundred and sixteen have been scrapped since 2006.
So that is about fourteen thousand short of the first target. Where did the gap come from? Here are the possible reasons.
Money moved. In 2024 Treasury moved one hundred and sixteen million rand out of the programme, citing lower spending and other pressures, including inauguration payments.
Numbers differ. In 2022 the Mail and Guardian reported that the department's figures did not match its own annual reports.
Corruption? We found no Auditor-General, SIU or court finding, so that is not proven. It is a question the department must answer.
One study says the programme replaces old vehicles but does not tackle destructive competition over routes, so the biggest national taxi spend does not aim at what starts the wars.
So what happens next?
On the twenty sixth of October, arrests were made, and the accused were charged with murder and arson.
On the twenty ninth, the MEC, the City, SANTACO and CODETA met, but without CATA.
Whether these talks bring lasting peace is not yet known.

scenes.headline: The short answer
points: Routes mean money, so groups fight
lines: So here is the short answer.
Routes are worth a lot of money, so groups fight over them.
The licence system is weak, and many hands share the blame.
And too few people behind the violence face real consequences.

scenes.headline: Stay safe and be heard

steps.title: Check before you travel
steps.sub: Look for route closure and go-slow news

steps.title: Have a backup plan
steps.sub: Tell your boss early if you may be late

steps.title: Ask your councillor for answers
steps.sub: Ask what is being done about your rank

lines: You cannot end a taxi war alone, but there are steps you can take.
Check the news and closure notices before you leave home.
If you see a crime or get a threat, report it to the police.
Plan a backup way to work, and tell your employer early if you may be late.
And ask your ward councillor what is being done about your local rank.

items.title: Start a commuter group
items.sub: Share safe routes and updates by WhatsApp

items.title: Go to ward meetings
items.sub: Ask for rank safety and clear answers

items.title: Talk to local employers
items.sub: Ask for flexible hours on bad days

items.title: Demand updates on the talks
items.sub: Ask the province and City to report back

lines: Together, a community has more power.
Start a commuter group to share safe routes and updates.
Go to ward meetings and ask for rank safety and clear answers.
Talk to local employers about flexible hours on bad days, and keep asking the province and City for updates.
